subject: How to predict shape with PLS

messages.author: 96a78639336ed702
messages.subject: How to predict shape with PLS
parts:
In page 119 of user manual of geomorph v3.1.2, shape prediction with PLS was performed with the following code:

data(plethShapeFood)
Y.gpa<-gpagen(plethShapeFood$land) #GPA-alignment
# 2B-PLS between head shape and food use data
PLS <-two.b.pls(A1 = plethShapeFood$food, A2 = Y.gpa$coords, iter=999)
summary(PLS)
plot(PLS)




preds <- shape.predictor(Y.gpa$coords, plethShapeFood$food, Intercept = FALSE,
method = "PLS", pred1 = 2, pred2 = -4, pred3 = 2.5) # using PLS plot as a guide

I have several questions on shape prediction with PLS:

1. If I want to understand what shape features are associated with a PLS component, say PLS component 3, of the shape matrix A2, I think I could plot shape at +2SD and -2SD of that PLS component and visualize shape differences. I noted that the object PLS contains left/right vectors, X/YScores, and svd, which contains d, u, and vt. I wish to know how could I make use of the ouput of PLS to plot shape at +2 SD of PLS component 3 of the shape matrix A2?

2. If I want to understand shape features associated with PLS component, say PLS component 2, of the predictor matrix A1, following the previous line of thought, I may need to predict plethodon shape corresponding to +2SD and -2SD of PLS component 2 of A1 and then visualize shape differences. But again, how could I make use of the ouput of PLS to plot shape at +2 SD of PLS component 2 of the shape matrix A1?

3. Although I could see the location of 2, -4, and 2.5 along PLS1 Block 1 from the above plot, I wish to know in a study, how should I determine the value of meaningful predictors to choose when method is set to "PLS"? Put it another way, how should I interpret the predicted shape at predictor value of 2, -4, and 2.5?

Thank you!

messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] How to predict shape with PLS
parts:
Yes this can be done.   The trick is to give shape.predictor the PLS scores directly, rather than asking it to compute them (when it computes, it uses PLS1 as per the help file).

 

This is the standard approach for PLS-1

preds <- shape.predictor(Y.gpa$coords, plethShapeFood$food, Intercept = FALSE,

                         method = "PLS", pred1 = 2, pred2 = -4, pred3 = 2.5) # using PLS plot as a guide

Here is the approach for PLS-2: NOTE: one must perform the PLS ahead of time, and provide the scores from that.

 

preds2 <- shape.predictor(Y.gpa$coords, PLS$XScores[,2], Intercept = FALSE,

                         method = "LS", pred1 = 2, pred2 = -4, pred3 = 2.5) # using PLS plot as a guide

 

Notice also that one changes method to ‘LS’ rather than ‘PLS’ because the PLS was pre-computed.

 

As to your last question, determining meaningful values for the predicted shapes is a case-by-case basis. For a continuous variable, we often look towards the extremes of our data distribution along the regression or correlation plot. To do this, one must identify them via visual inspection, as you correct determined was the case for the two extremes used in the example. There is not an automatic way for this at present: human intervention is required, and in fact encouraged, as only the researcher knows what they wish to plot!

 

Dean

Dear Prof. Dean

Thank you very much for your insightful suggestions.

Following your hints, I would like to confirm that I am right in the two points below:

1. To visualize shape differences between two extremes of PLS-3 of shape matrix A2:

preds2 <- shape.predictor(Y.gpa$coords, PLS$YScores[,3], Intercept = FALSE,

                         method = "LS", pred1 = min(PLS$YScores[,3]), pred2 = max(PLS$YScores[,3])) # using PLS plot as a guide


plotRefToTarget(preds2$pred1, preds2$pred2)


2. To visualize shape differences between two extremes of PLS-2 of the predictor matrix A1:

preds3 <- shape.predictor(Y.gpa$coords, PLS$XScores[,2], Intercept = FALSE,

                         method = "LS", pred1 = min(PLS$XScores[,2]), pred2 = max(PLS$XScores[,2])) # using PLS plot as a guide


plotRefToTarget(preds3$pred1, preds3$pred2)


Best regards,
Patrick
